chunks.title: Lenin's death and Lenin's legacy, 1924
chunks.body:
Lenin died on **21 January 1924**, after three strokes. For more than a year before his death, the party had governed without him. Against his own wishes, the Politburo embalmed his body and displayed it in a mausoleum on Red Square, and Petrograd became Leningrad. Lenin became a cult, and every contender for power claimed to be his most loyal follower. As one historian puts it, each "invented his own Lenin to suit his purposes".

Lenin's own judgement was a danger to **Stalin**. In notes dictated in December 1922 and January 1923, later called his "Testament", Lenin wrote that "Stalin is too rude" and urged his removal as General Secretary. But the Testament also criticised **Trotsky** for "excessive self-assurance". When the notes were read to the Central Committee in May 1924, Stalin was protected by a **triumvirate** with **Zinoviev** and **Kamenev**, who were more afraid of Trotsky, and the issue was sidetracked at the Thirteenth Party Congress.

Trotsky had other weaknesses. He had clashed with Lenin before 1917 and joined the Bolsheviks only in mid-1917, so he was at a disadvantage in arguments about who was the truest Leninist. When he struck back in November 1924 with "The Lessons of October", reminding the party that Zinoviev and Kamenev had opposed the October rising, he only deepened his rivals' hostility.

This mattered because the succession was fought in the language of loyalty to Lenin, which meant that Stalin's apparently dull post as General Secretary, and his rivals' fear of Trotsky, counted for more than Lenin's warning.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Lenin's cult made loyalty to Lenin the test of leadership.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was an alliance of convenience.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Lenin's legacy was a weapon that Stalin used better than his rivals.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The Testament of 1922–23 urged Stalin's removal, yet in May 1924 the triumvirate of Stalin, Zinoviev and Kamenev sidetracked it at the Thirteenth Congress.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Stalin survived the greatest threat to his career because his allies feared Trotsky more than him.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Testament also criticised Trotsky, and Trotsky's late entry into the Bolsheviks weakened his claim to be Lenin's heir.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Lenin's legacy therefore helped Stalin, because his rivals could not use it against him without damaging themselves.

chunks.title: The machine and the debate, 1924–1926
chunks.body:
Stalin's office gave him a quiet but decisive advantage. When he became **General Secretary** in 1922, the Secretariat was not a prestigious body, and Stalin seemed to lack the brilliance and oratory of a party leader. But it let him bring supporters of "the party line" into the central apparatus and control appointments in the provinces. Factions had been banned since 1921.

The contest was also about policy. In the **industrialisation debate** of 1923–27, all leaders wanted industry, but they disagreed about how fast and at whose expense. The economist Preobrazhenskii, linked to Trotsky's **Left Opposition**, argued for "super-industrialisation" financed by squeezing the peasants. **Bukharin** argued that the Soviet Union could "grow into socialism" through a steady link (*smychka*) with the peasantry under the New Economic Policy (NEP). Stalin sided with Bukharin and championed "socialism in one country", which made Trotsky's "permanent revolution" look like a lack of faith in the USSR.

Stalin moved against his rivals one at a time. Trotsky lost control of the Red Army's Revolutionary Military Council in January 1925. By the end of 1925 Zinoviev and Kamenev had broken with Stalin and were criticising his ambitions, but at the Fourteenth Congress in December 1925 they were outvoted. In early 1926 they joined Trotsky in the **United Opposition**, demanding freer debate, an end to NEP and faster industrialisation.

This mattered because Stalin combined control of the party machine with a popular, moderate policy, which meant that his opponents appeared both divisive and dangerous.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Secretariat was not prestigious at first.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin's moderate policy isolated the Left.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He later adopted much of the Left's programme.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin defeated rivals one at a time.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The United Opposition united them too late.

chunks.title: Defeat of the Left, 1926–1929
chunks.body:
The United Opposition never threatened Stalin's majority. Its leaders demanded the freedom to argue inside the party, but the ban on factions made organised opposition illegal. Its programme had defenders: the historian Vadim Rogovin argues that its 1927 proposals for worker representation would have developed democracy in the workplace. But in **November 1927**, after the Opposition held its own street demonstration on the tenth anniversary of the revolution, **Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled** from the party. The Fifteenth Congress in December 1927 completed the defeat.

The defeated responded differently. Zinoviev and Kamenev recanted and were readmitted in 1928, though they never regained their influence. Trotsky refused to capitulate. In early 1928 he was exiled to a remote region, and in **February 1929** he was expelled from the Soviet Union altogether.

Stalin had now removed the Left, and his alliance with Bukharin had served its purpose. Over the next two years he would turn against the Right as well.

This mattered because Stalin used the party's own rules against unity to destroy his rivals, which meant that by 1928 no organised opposition was left on the Left.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The ban on factions made opposition illegal.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Opposition leaders were still party members until 1927.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Trotsky's refusal to recant led to exile.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Stalin defeated the United Opposition because the party's rules made organised opposition illegal.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Factions had been banned since 1921, and in November 1927, after the Opposition's own demonstration, Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the Opposition could be presented as splitting the party, so its leaders lost their membership rather than an argument.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Rogovin argues that its programme offered genuine democratic proposals, which suggests it was defeated by organisation rather than ideas.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The Left was therefore defeated mainly by the party's own discipline, which Stalin controlled.

chunks.title: Turning on the Right and the 'Great Change', 1928–1929
chunks.body:
With the Left gone, Stalin changed course. In the winter of 1927–28 grain procurements fell short, and Stalin personally supervised "extraordinary" (coercive) measures to seize grain in the Urals and western Siberia. This broke with Bukharin's policy of conciliating the peasants. The industrialisation debate had already shown the logic: once the Left was defeated, a faster tempo of heavy industry became politically attractive, and that meant more pressure on the countryside.

**Bukharin**, **Rykov** and **Tomsky** resisted, and in 1928 Stalin attacked their "rightist deviation". Between 1928 and 1930 they were sidelined and removed from their key posts. By 1927 the Politburo already contained men such as Molotov and Kaganovich, who would stand beside Stalin throughout the 1930s.

In November 1929, on the twelfth anniversary of the revolution, *Pravda* published Stalin's article **"A Year of Great Change"**. It justified a radical break with NEP and served as a manifesto for the First Five-Year Plan, already in its second year. Stalin had adopted much of the Left's programme after defeating the Left, and destroyed the Right by attacking the policy he had once defended.

This mattered because Stalin's flexibility over policy served one constant aim, power, which meant that by the end of 1929 he faced no organised opposition at the top of the party.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin turned on the Right once the Left was defeated.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He had defended NEP with Bukharin until 1927.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Coercion of the peasants signalled the change.
By 1929 Stalin had broken with NEP.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Five-Year Plan was already under way.

useItInAnEssay.test: However, Stalin's change of course was also a response to real grain shortages, not only to the struggle for power.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Stalin therefore used policy as a weapon, changing it to isolate whichever rival remained.

modelPlan.thesis: Stalin defeated the Left because he controlled the party majority, the 1921 ban on factions made opposition illegal, and his rivals were divided until 1926; the result was the expulsion of the Opposition and Stalin's freedom to turn on the Right.

arguments.claim: Reason: the ban on factions and rivals' divisions.
Result: the turn against the Right.

modelPlan.counter: Rogovin argues the Opposition's programme was genuinely democratic, so its defeat was not a defeat of its ideas.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? Stalin's freedom to turn on the Right.

segments.text: Stalin defeated the Left mainly because he controlled the party majority and its rules.
Factions had been banned since 1921, and in November 1927, after the Opposition's own demonstration, Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled.
This meant that the Opposition was defeated as a breach of discipline rather than in argument, so its leaders recanted or were exiled.
However, the Left also weakened itself: Zinoviev and Kamenev helped Stalin against Trotsky in 1924 and united with him only in 1926.
The most significant result was therefore that Stalin, free of the Left, could turn on Bukharin and the Right.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the political positions of Trotsky and Bukharin between 1924 and 1929.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.judgement: Where did they agree, and why did both lose?

modelPlan.thesis: Trotsky and Bukharin held opposite economic positions, rapid industrialisation at the peasants' expense against 'growing into socialism' through NEP, but both were defeated by Stalin, who used each against the other and then adopted Trotsky's programme without Trotsky.

arguments.claim: Difference: permanent revolution versus socialism in one country.
Similarity: both defeated by Stalin's majority.

modelPlan.counter: By 1928 Bukharin too opposed Stalin's methods, which brought the two former opponents closer.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Why did both lose? Because Stalin controlled the majority and changed policy to isolate each.

segments.text: Trotsky and Bukharin stood at opposite ends of the debate, but they shared the same fate.
Trotsky's Left wanted rapid industrialisation financed by squeezing the peasants, whereas Bukharin defended NEP and 'growing into socialism' through the smychka.
This meant that Stalin could ally with Bukharin to defeat Trotsky in 1927, and then turn on Bukharin's 'rightist deviation' in 1928.
However, both were also defeated because they relied on argument while Stalin controlled the party majority.
Their positions were therefore opposed, but their defeats were alike: each was isolated by Stalin's shifting alliances.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the role of Lenin's legacy in the struggle for power between 1924 and 1929.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Lenin's legacy shaped the struggle as a contest over loyalty to Lenin; it threatened Stalin through the Testament, but Stalin turned it into a weapon by presenting 'socialism in one country' as Leninist and Trotsky as a late convert.

arguments.claim: Trotsky's past and the Lessons of October.
The ban on factions as Lenin's rule.

modelPlan.counter: The Testament criticised all the leading contenders, so it could not decide the succession by itself.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Weapon or obstacle? An obstacle to Stalin in 1924, a weapon for him thereafter.

segments.text: Lenin's legacy was both a threat to Stalin and his most useful weapon.
Lenin's Testament urged Stalin's removal, but in May 1924 the triumvirate sidetracked it, and Stalin presented 'socialism in one country' as consistent with Lenin's outlook.
This meant that the contest was fought over who was the truest Leninist, so Trotsky, who joined the Bolsheviks only in 1917, was at a disadvantage.
However, Lenin's legacy did not decide the outcome alone: the Testament also criticised Trotsky, and the votes were won through the apparatus.
Lenin's legacy therefore framed the struggle, and Stalin used that frame better than his rivals.
